Passes over a `parquetExprStore` that cannot hold the whole store in memory read
it in **cell windows**.

A pass windows when an intermediate would otherwise scale with the data rather
than with the answer — in practice, when a grouping puts a join in front of an
otherwise small aggregate. Windowing bounds that join's input; it does not change
the result, because the accumulators are additive over cells.

That is the whole idea. The rest of this article is why it has to be the cell
axis, when it kicks in, what it costs, and why the work is not simply handed to a
query engine — which is the reasonable first question and the one with the least
obvious answer.

`storeChunkInfo()` reports the numbers for a given store on the current machine,
and carries the two options. The decision is recorded in
`adr/0011-cell-windowing-over-spill.md`.

## Which passes window, and why

Several passes window, and they do it for two different reasons — worth
separating, because only one of them is about rescuing a plan that would
otherwise fail.

Traced with the window pinned small enough to force several:

| pass | windows | folds | why it windows |
|---|---|---|---|
| `processData(normParam("library"))` | no | – | records an op; nothing is scanned |
| `analyzeData(featStatsParam)`, ungrouped, lowerable chain | no | – | one streamed plan, bounded by the engine |
| `analyzeData(featStatsParam, groups = )` | yes | yes | **to bound the grouping join** |
| `analyzeData(featStatsParam)` with `@post_ops` | yes | yes | the chain must run on materialized rows |
| `reduceData(pcaParam("random"))` | yes | no | reads a sparse chunk per window |
| `reduceData(gramEigenPcaParam())` | yes | no | same, plus one band per worker |
| `storeWrite()` bake | yes | no | builds and writes a chunk at a time |

**Materializing passes** — PCA, the `storeWrite()` bake, and the `@post_ops`
accumulator — window because they build something per chunk by nature: a sparse
matrix, or a collected triplet frame. They were always going to read in pieces,
and the window only decides how big a piece. Nothing here rescues them; it sizes
them.

**The grouped statistic is the one exception**, and the only case where the
alternative is not "slower" but "fails". It has a perfectly good streaming plan;
what it does not have is a bound on the join in front of the aggregate. That is
what the rest of this article is about.

An ungrouped statistic on a lowerable chain does not window at all — one
streamed plan, the scan never retained, bounded by the engine however large the
store is.

Folding is a separate axis. Only the two accumulator paths fold, because only
they produce partials that combine by addition. PCA and the bake write each
window into a slice nothing else touches, so there is nothing to combine and no
reassociation to worry about.

## What forces a window: the grouping join

A grouped statistic is taken per (feature, group) rather than per feature. To
get there, a per-cell group assignment has to be joined onto the values before
the aggregate runs.

The aggregate itself stays small — features × groups, so tens of thousands of
rows for a whole transcriptome against twenty clusters. The **join in front of
it** does not: it emits one row per stored value. That intermediate scales with
the data rather than with the answer, and Arrow's engine has no spill-to-disk
path, so past a certain size the pass does not slow down. It fails.

Windowing removes that intermediate rather than finding somewhere to put it.
Each window's join feeds its own aggregate and is released before the next
window begins, so the large frame is never assembled at all.

On a 5,000 × 50,000 store at 3% density (7.5M stored values), 12 groups:

| execution | engine peak | elapsed |
|---|---|---|
| whole store, one plan | 187 MB | 0.20 s |
| 20 cell windows | 44 MB | 1.60 s |

Same results to the last bit for counts, and to within a few ULP for
floating-point sums (see *Reproducibility*). The memory figure is Arrow's own
allocator high-water mark, measured one variant per process — process RSS is
dominated by loaded namespaces at this scale and tells you nothing useful.

## When it happens

Automatically, and only when needed. The window is derived per read, never
stored:

```
bytes per cell = features × density × bytes per stored value
budget         = free RAM × giottodisk.chunk_ram_frac      (default 0.25)
window         = min(cells, max(10000, budget / bytes per cell))
```

So a pass windows exactly when the whole view would not fit the budget. When it
would fit, `window` comes back as the full cell count, the loop runs once, and
the pass *is* the single plan it always was. There is no branch and no mode —
see *Not a mode*.

A worked case. 19,000 features at 6% density is roughly 55 kB per cell. Half a
million cells is then about 27 GB of payload, against a ~1 GB budget on an 8 GB
machine: around 27 windows. The same features over 40,000 cells fit in one
window and behave exactly as they did before windowing existed.

`storeChunkInfo()` reports these numbers for a given store on the current
machine, for both read shapes.

Two details worth knowing:

- The `10000` is a **floor, not a guarantee**. On very wide data a 10,000-cell
  window can still exceed the budget, and no smaller window will be chosen.
- Sizing needs the store's density. A store built straight from a path by
  `parquetExprStore()` — where `scan_stats = FALSE` is the default — has no
  cached marginals and must count its nonzeros first, which costs one extra
  pass. Stores from `storeWrite()` and the convenience importers carry
  marginals already, and they survive `snapshotSave()` / `snapshotLoad()`.

## Why the cell axis, and not features

A window is a contiguous range of **cells**, and that is not a free choice.

Stores are written cell-major — sorted by `(row_id, col_id)`, where `row_id` is
the cell. A contiguous cell range therefore narrows to a simple range predicate
that lets the parquet reader skip whole row groups. Each window reads only its
own slice, so N windows still cost one pass over the data.

Narrowing by feature cannot do that. Features are not the sort key, so every row
group holds every feature and a feature-side predicate prunes nothing. The batch
reads the whole store and throws away most of it.

This matters because feature batching is the workaround people reach for first —
ask for 250 genes, loop over blocks, stay inside memory. It buys the same
bound at a far worse price, and the cost is **linear in the number of batches**,
not in the genes per batch. Measured on the store above:

| feature batch | passes | elapsed |
|---|---|---|
| 250 genes | 20 | 1.77 s |
| 500 genes | 10 | 0.57 s |
| 1000 genes | 5 | 0.31 s |

Four times fewer batches, four times faster, regardless of how many genes each
one covers — the signature of every batch rescanning the store. Extrapolated to
556M stored values, 76 feature batches is on the order of twenty minutes where
one windowed pass is tens of seconds.

Ask for every feature at once and let the window do the bounding.

## Why not one engine pass

The data is parquet. Both Arrow's engine and DuckDB will run a grouped aggregate
over parquet unaided, and DuckDB will do it without running out of memory. The
reason not to is not that they cannot — it is that the plan they would run is the
wrong one for this statistic.

### Arrow (Acero)

Not a choice against Acero — Acero is what executes each window. It handles the
joinless aggregates end to end, which is exactly why ungrouped statistics never
window.

What it cannot do is bound the grouping join. Having no spill path, the
whole-store version of that plan does not degrade gracefully — it dies. That
failure is useful, though, because it is not really a memory problem: the plan
builds one row per stored value to return one row per (feature, group), and
nothing between those two ever needed to exist. Acero's strictness is what turned
a wasteful plan into a visible one.

### DuckDB

DuckDB would survive the same plan, because its joins and aggregates spill to
disk. But surviving is all it buys, and it is worth being precise about why that
is not enough.

Spilling means materializing the large intermediate, writing it out, and reading
it back. Windowing means never building it. For a sum, a count, or a sum of
squares — statistics that are exactly additive over cells — nothing needs to
exist all at once, so paying to store and re-read it is work with no result
attached. Windowing also prunes, as above: each window touches only its own row
groups, where one pass reads everything.

Put bluntly: spill is the right tool when an aggregate genuinely cannot be
decomposed — a rank, a median, anything needing every value in view at once. A
sum of squares is not that. Spilling would make the materializing plan survive;
it would not make it the right plan, which is also why a future engine that
spills is not a reason to revisit this.

Two further practical limits, for anyone tempted to wire it up:

- The R-side steps of an op chain (`@post_ops`) have no SQL form at all, so a
  chain that has left the query engine cannot be handed to one.
- A spilling engine still has to be given a memory limit, and that limit is the
  same number the window is derived from. The sizing problem does not go away.

There is also a wiring detail specific to this class. `parquetExprStore` extends
`queryableStore`, not `parquetStore`, so `storeRead(output = "duckdb")` reaches
the Arrow-backed bridge (`duckdb_register_arrow`) rather than DuckDB's native
`read_parquet` scanner — Arrow stays the reader, and DuckDB's memory limit never
sees Arrow's allocation. The native SQL path exists in the package for tabular
and geometry stores, but it is not wired to expression stores, and wiring it
would require rendering the axis predicates as SQL. Skipping that step returns
the un-subset store with no error.

### Where an engine genuinely wins

The case windowing cannot serve at all: a statistic needing a **global ordering
along the feature axis** — a rank, a median, a Wilcoxon test. No combination of
per-window results reconstructs a rank, and the store's layout cannot prune the
axis it would need. That is the shape worth reaching for a spilling engine for,
and it has no streaming path today. `analyzeData(x, scranMarkersParam)` refuses
`test_type = "wilcox"` for exactly this reason.

## Not a mode

There is no chunked mode and no unchunked mode, and neither option switches one
on. The window loop always runs; when the budget covers the view it yields a
single window.

In particular, pinning `giottodisk.chunk_size` large does not make a pass
"unchunked" — it removes the memory bound that keeps the pass from failing on a
large store. Reach for it when you know the data fits.

```r
# Both options change the bound, not the code path.
options(giottodisk.chunk_ram_frac = 0.10)  # budget less RAM per window
options(giottodisk.chunk_size = 25000)     # pin the window in cells
```

`giottodisk.chunk_ram_frac` is the one to reach for first: it scales every pass
without needing to know any store's shape. `giottodisk.chunk_size` is an escape
hatch — for a machine whose free memory cannot be read, a shape the model sizes
badly, or a test that needs to force several windows.

Neither is a performance dial. A smaller window lowers peak memory and adds
per-window overhead; a larger one does the reverse. The derived value is already
the largest window the budget allows, which is the fastest one that stays
bounded. Measured on the store above, per-window overhead is roughly 45–65 ms:
one window 0.27 s, twenty windows 1.60 s, fifty windows 2.29 s.

## Why the window is not stored

The window is derived on every read rather than recorded on the object, because
it depends on free RAM — a property of the machine doing the reading, not of the
data. Baking one in at write time would make it stale the moment the store moved
to a different machine.

What *is* machine-independent is the payload size per stored value, and that is
what the `@stats` marginals cache. Sizing then costs arithmetic rather than a
scan — provided the marginals are there, which is the case noted under *When it
happens*.

## Reproducibility

The window count comes from free RAM **at call time**, so it is a property of
the machine and the moment, not of the store, and it can differ between runs.

Combining window parts is exact for counts. For floating-point sums it
reassociates the addition, so a float statistic can differ by a few units in the
last place between runs with different window counts — measured 2–3 ULP, maximum
relative difference around 3e-16. Results are reproducible to **tolerance, not
bitwise**: compare them with a tolerance rather than hashing them or
snapshotting exact digits.

This is fifteen significant figures in and invisible to analysis, with one
thing worth keeping in view: a **discrete** choice taken on a float statistic —
a top-N feature selection, a threshold comparison — can in principle land
differently if two candidates are separated by less than that. Ties that close
are not meaningful distinctions, but they can move a downstream result keyed to
the selection.

In the current pipeline that risk does not arise, because the only windowed
statistics are the grouped ones, and those sit *downstream* of clustering rather
than upstream of it. Normalization lowers to `@ops`, which keeps the ungrouped
statistics — including the variance that feature selection ranks on — on the
single-plan path. If an op ever lands on `@post_ops`, that changes: the
ungrouped accumulator becomes windowed, and a discrete feature cut then sits
downstream of a reassociated float sum. Check selection stability across window
counts before assuming it does not matter.

## PCA windows too, differently

The PCA passes read cell windows for the same reason — a chunk at a time keeps
peak memory at one window's worth — but they do not use the additive fold
described above. Each window writes into a disjoint slice of a preallocated
result, or accumulates into a running matrix product. There is no partial to
combine, so the reassociation question does not arise, and PCA output is
bitwise reproducible across window counts.

The parallel band workers add one more level: the cell axis is split into one
band per worker, then into windows within each band. Bands are disjoint row
ranges, so each worker writes its own slice and the partials need no
reconciliation.
